analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance plan competing with private plans on the ACA marketplaces.
analysis.headline: The public option bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Affordable Care Act to have the Department of Health and Human Services offer its own health insurance plan through the ACA marketplaces, in every state, alongside private plans. It would have to follow the same rules as private marketplace plans, offer bronze, silver, and gold tiers, and set premiums high enough to pay for its own costs, with $2 billion in start-up funding that it must repay over ten years. For the first three years it would pay doctors and hospitals Medicare rates plus a 5% bonus, and after that it could use payment methods designed to reward efficient care. The idea was that a lower-priced public plan would compete with private insurers and push premiums down for people buying their own coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance on the ACA marketplaces, especially those who earn too much for premium subsidies and pay full price. They would get a new, lower-cost plan to choose from, and private insurers would face pressure to lower their own prices to compete. People with no marketplace plans in their area would also gain, since the public option would be offered nationwide.

how_it_helps.text: The public option would be offered in every state through the ACA exchanges, guaranteeing at least one plan choice everywhere [S2][S3].
Its premiums would be set at a level that fully covers health benefits and administrative costs, with no profit margin added, making it structurally cheaper than private plans [S3].
For 2015 through 2017 it would pay providers at Medicare rates plus a 5% bonus, lower than typical private-plan rates, which is how the plan would keep premiums down [S2][S3].

It would have to comply with the same rules as private marketplace plans, including the same benefits, provider network standards, and consumer protections, so it would compete on a level playing field [S2][S3].
An ombudsman office would handle complaints from enrollees, and the plan would have to collect data to help reduce racial and ethnic health disparities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers, who would lose customers to a cheaper competitor and could see their marketplace premiums driven down. Hospitals and doctors would be paid Medicare-level rates rather than higher private rates for public-option patients, though with a 5% bonus in the first three years. Taxpayers would front $2 billion in start-up funding plus initial claims reserves, which the plan must repay over ten years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The plan starts with $2 billion of appropriated start-up funding plus 90 days of claims reserves, and while the bill requires repayment over ten years, taxpayers bear the risk if enrollment or costs miss projections [S3].

Medicare-level payment rates are lower than what private insurers pay, so hospitals and physicians could respond by shifting costs onto other patients or limiting how many public-option patients they treat.
The bill bars any administrative or judicial review of the payment rates and methods the Secretary sets, which removes a check on how the plan pays providers [S3].

Because the plan is the government competing with private companies while also writing its competitors' regulatory rules, critics argued it would not compete on equal terms; the bill addresses this by subjecting the plan to the same exchange requirements as private plans [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people paying full price for marketplace coverage, the upside is real: a no-profit government plan paying Medicare-level rates would likely undercut private premiums, and the competitive pressure alone could lower prices across the marketplace. The main costs fall on insurers and providers in the form of lower revenue, and on taxpayers in the form of start-up funding that must be repaid. The bill is moderately designed: it forces the plan to self-finance, uses the same exchange rules as private plans, and includes a 5% provider bonus to build networks, though the bar on reviewing its payment decisions is a real weakness. The tradeoff is mostly a question of whether the country wants government as a health insurer, which is a values dispute the bill never got to have.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to its Health Subcommittee a week later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the Public Option Deficit Reduction Act on January 9, 2015, with 27 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and to that committee's Health Subcommittee on January 16, 2015 [S5].
That was the last action of any kind. The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S5].
The bill had 37 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, and Republicans controlled the House, the committee, and its Health Subcommittee throughout the 114th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers were better off because the bill died: the exchange market stayed entirely theirs, with no government plan to compete against. Marketplace customers who wanted a cheaper public option got nothing. Taxpayers avoided the start-up funding risk, and hospitals kept private-rate payments for all patients.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a public health insurance option on the ACA exchanges.

for.name: 37 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 37 cosponsors were Democrats, and none was a committee chair who could schedule action on it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by Republicans in the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on January 16, 2015, and took no further action on it for the remaining two years of the Congress; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled [S5].

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows no committee action after the subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 37 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-led committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: A government plan paying Medicare-level rates with no profit margin would compete directly with private marketplace plans, drawing away customers and pressuring their premiums down. Insurers' interest in keeping the exchange market to themselves runs against cheaper coverage for marketplace shoppers.

The public option would pay hospitals Medicare rates rather than higher private rates for its enrollees, cutting revenue, though a 5% bonus would apply for the first three years and hospitals participating in Medicare would automatically be in-network unless they opt out. Lower insurance costs for patients come partly at hospitals' expense.

Doctors in the public option would accept Medicare-level rates plus a 5% first-three-year bonus, with a choice of accepting the rate as payment in full or limiting extra charges. Like hospitals, they would trade some revenue for a large new pool of patients.

Drugs not covered under Medicare parts A or B would be paid at rates the Secretary negotiates, a lever private plans also use but that a government plan could push harder, with savings flowing to lower premiums.
